To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the velocity dispersion of a galaxy cluster is a good mass estimator, and (2) the scatter in the velocity dispersion-mass relation is ~30%.
we have measured velocity dispersions for 48 galaxy clusters, and that these dispersions are in agreement with those expected for dark-matter-only cosmological simulations.

(a) the velocity dispersion of a cluster can be measured with a precision of 10% from 15 member galaxies, and (b) the observed dispersion of SPT clusters is consistent with the expectation from dark matter simulations
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of galaxy clusters as a tool for cosmological studies.
the use of the South Pole Telescope to detect galaxy clusters.
the properties of the intergalactic medium (IGM) in clusters and groups of galaxies and the relation of the IGM to the properties of the galaxies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have not detected any significant deviation from the predictions of Λ cold dark matter.
the velocity dispersions and masses of SPT-discovered clusters are in good agreement with those expected from dark-mattersimulated clusters.
our measurements are consistent with the expectations from simulations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the velocity dispersion-mass scaling relation is well understood, with a small systematic uncertainty, and a small amount of scatter.
we find the scaling relations of the velocity dispersion with mass and SZ observables are consistent with the expectations from dark-matter-only simulations.
we have found that the scaling relation between the velocity dispersions and the mass estimated from SZ and X-rays are consistent with expectations from simulations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SPT-SXCS cluster catalog provides an excellent data set for studying scaling relations of galaxy cluster observables.
velocity dispersions of SZE-selected clusters can be used as an accurate and robust mass estimator, provided that the velocity dispersion is measured using at least 15 galaxies.
velocity dispersions measured from optical spectra of cluster members can provide a robust mass estimate for SZ-selected galaxy clusters, with a scatter comparable to the SZ mass estimate.
